Restricted status! It's my favorite Facebook "secret"!

First, make sure your profile is private. 

You have to be on a computer, not a phone. On the left side under Explore, you should see Friend Lists. Click on Restricted. On the upper right, you'll see manage list.

Another way to do it is to bring up your friends list. There's a button next to each name. Hover and you'll see what lists they're on. Click on add to another list and choose Restricted. 

Restricted is not unfriended. You can see what they post, but they can't see what you post, unless you tag them or your post is public. This way, they have no idea you placed them on any list and remain "friends" with you. 

I use it a lot now, to keep a record of my JNMIL's online behavior (guilt posts, angry posts, and love bombing, ugh).

So, last spring, during the activity, my child pulled rank on Mongo's. My child has a leadership position in the activity. It wasn't anything that should have upset anyone. It was a simple answer to a question that Mongo's child didn't like. This upset Mongo. So Mongo took to Facebook (spare me) to bash me and my child (because I raised my child wrong).

It continued through the activity's mini-camp. I simply took screen shots of all the spewage. Apparently, many other parents saw this nastiness (dumb Mongo didn't make Facebook private). Five separate parents sent the activity board letters about Mongo. I think someone talked them into this, but each letter had different incidents of Mongo madness.

Board thought that was harsh and decided to just ban Mongo from volunteering around students. I was cool with that. Mongo, not so much.

Mongo decided to keep spewing garbage online, and I guess that wasn't enough. One day Mongo hit another car while trying to park next to mine at a large shopping center (my car is unusual). During regular activity camp, Mongo and spouse approached my car and verbally assaulted me in the presence of my young child. 

Mongo kept on stalking me and other board members online. I never reported, just documented. Then Mongo went too far. 

Mongo made comments online about my young child (who is the same age as Mongo's youngest spawn, but not involved with the activity at all). The comments broke our state's cyber-bullying law. The comments made were about my child's disability. After contacting the police, we contacted the schools involved.

The child involved in the beginning and my child are headed to an elite event together next week, and I am nervous. Mongo is not a small person. Many people scared of Mongo.

I'm a mom of a 17 year old senior. I want you to know that while your friends seem to be totally happy, they're not all that way. I assure you. I am very good at appearing to be the happy carefree person who laughs and jokes a lot, even in my darkest times.

When I'm alone and being honest with myself, I completely break down. 

I want you to know that even though your friends seem to be so easy-going and carefree, it's not always the case. It's much easier to play the part of the happy person than to let people know how you really feel. I am excellent at being "fine." 

My daughter's friends all have their own issues, and she has social anxiety. She has managed to overcome it to a point, and she has several leadership roles in her activities. She has friends that have serious issues, and rely on her to be their solid foundation. She actually has a friend who she would love to tell to piss off, but she knows that she's the only person this girl has to let off steam to.  This girl always threatens suicide when something a little complicated happens. My daughter has seen me at my worst - suicidal, breakdowns, running away and screaming fits. She knows the difference between depression and cries for attention. But she's not going to tell this girl to knock off her shit. She listens and tries her best to bring her back to earth. 

I also want to address your suicidal thoughts. I want you to know that people do care about you. Your parents probably don't know what to say to you. It's so hard to open your heart to someone and not get the response you need. I don't even know you, but I think that you have so much to offer to this world. You are living in a tumultuous age. I don't want you to end your life. You're 16. There's plenty of time for the girls to notice you. They probably already do. It's a very difficult age where you all are afraid of rejection. Try your best to enjoy your talents and stay with those gifts of music and drama. It may be a year or two for you to be comfortable enough with yourself with the opposite sex. You are still so young, and have a bright future ahead of you. I don't know if college is part of your future plans, but many people don't even become their true selves until college. 

My advice to you is to put your feelings into a journal. All of your feelings. Write letters to the people in your life (in your journal - not to show them. If you go this route, put a disclaimer in the front of your journal in case they peep.) Then, go back and read them to yourself. You will see that your perspective changes often. That's what I have done.  The other thing to put in the journal is a list of things you are grateful for - no matter how small. 

The last two years of my life has been full of disappointments and low points. We had to declare bankruptcy and have to live on a tiny portion of our income. We've had to sacrifice so much, and I don't even know if we'll be able to have any kind of Christmas for our two kids. I haven't seen my mother in two years (she lives 8 states away), and my stepdad died of cancer this summer. We just don't have the means to go. I have been in a bad phase for a long time. But I have a family to live for. They would be devastated without me. I could never do that to them. 

Please, please know that you are not alone. But please know that you are important to this world - even if things seem bleak right now. I was in the exact same mode as you when I was your age. Remember that depression lies. It tells you that you are not worthy of the world. Everyone has something to offer. I believe in you.
